questions.q: Is Brightfield Outdoor Supply, the company in this case study, a real business?
options: No — it's explicitly described as a fictional, illustrative composite scenario
Yes — it is a real, named outdoor-gear retailer
Yes — it is a real company whose name was changed for privacy
The lesson does not say whether it is real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Brightfield Outdoor Supply as fictional and illustrative, not a real company, consistent with this catalog's policy against presenting invented scenarios as real.

questions.q: What exposed Brightfield's underlying MDM problem, per this lesson?
options: A VP of Operations asked how many distinct wholesale customers the company had and got three different answers from three systems
A single employee accidentally deleted the customer database
The company had never made a single sale through any channel
A government audit required an immediate data purge
questions.explain: The disagreement between three systems' customer counts is what surfaced the lack of a formal master data definition, owner, and architecture style.

questions.q: In the Chapter 2 step of the walkthrough, what happened to matches that fell below the confidence threshold?
options: They were routed to a steward for manual review rather than merged automatically
They were deleted without any review
They were merged automatically regardless of confidence
They were ignored and left as permanent duplicates
questions.explain: Following Lesson 11's match-review practice, low-confidence matches went to a human steward instead of being auto-merged, avoiding incorrect consolidations.

questions.q: What reference data problem did the Chapter 4 step of the walkthrough fix?
options: Three systems used different codes for the same country or state/province (e.g. CA, CAN, and the spelled-out name), now unified under one governed code list
The company had no product catalog of any kind
All vendor records had already been perfectly deduplicated before this step
Reference data was deemed unnecessary and removed entirely
questions.explain: Drifted local code lists for country/state values were replaced with one managed, governed code list, with cross-reference tables mapping legacy codes during the transition.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why did the final fix at Brightfield actually work six months later?
options: There was exactly one record for each real customer, product, and vendor, everywhere — not because any one system got smarter
The company switched to using paper records instead of databases
All three original systems were simply shut down with no replacement
The VP of Operations manually recounted every customer by hand each month
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that consolidating to one record per real-world entity, not a smarter individual system, is what made the numbers finally agree.
